## TL;DR

The latest review found that a failed watchdog removal could delete the run's files and report a successful container removal. This follow-up preserves the files when removal is unconfirmed, reports the failure accurately, and quarantines the host before releasing its local slot. The same timeout and nonzero-exit handling now applies to operator-triggered removal.

## Work and rationale

The automatic hang recovery now treats only a completed Docker removal with exit code zero as confirmed. It starts remote bundle and artifact cleanup only after that confirmation. When removal times out, fails, or throws, it marks the host unhealthy before unblocking the run and releasing the local slot; the result and event no longer claim that the container was removed. The run still settles so a broken SSH connection cannot block the caller indefinitely.

The operator-triggered path had the same timeout classification issue. It now reports timeout as failure, avoids remote file cleanup on failure, and marks the host unhealthy before releasing the slot. The initial bookkeeping describes a removal request rather than claiming a kill before Docker responds.

Table-driven tests exercise both nonzero Docker exit and timeout for automatic and manual recovery, checking the returned status, retained files, and unhealthy host. Existing successful-removal tests cover cleanup and bounded recovery.

## Approaches tried

I traced the watchdog result through its transport race and checked the adjacent operator-triggered removal path. The first focused test run exposed a test mock that recursively called itself; retaining the original mock implementation fixed the fixture. The focused failure-path tests then passed.

## Challenges and blockers

A local slot must be released to settle a wedged SSH run, but doing so before the host is marked unhealthy can admit another job while the old container might still be alive. The ordering now explicitly marks the host unhealthy first. This session did not exercise a physical remote runner; the regression tests use simulated remote execution.

## Key learnings

A timeout or failed SSH command is not proof that Docker removed a container. Cleanup, operator-facing messages, and scheduling must all follow the confirmed removal outcome rather than the intent to kill.

The owner froze this task to the Tailscale runner path. After merging main, the watchdog now retains the run and slot when Docker removal fails; timeout and nonzero results are covered by a focused test. Remaining Docker and SSH failure-handling variants and provider parity are tracked in follow-up #1068.
